title: Act III, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: Lady Macbeth admits 'Nought's had, all's spent, where our desire is got without content.' She urges Macbeth to stop brooding. He says they have 'scotch'd the snake, not kill'd it,' that terrible dreams shake them nightly, and that Duncan in his grave sleeps well. 'O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife!' He hints at 'a deed of dreadful note' but tells her to 'be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck,' and calls on 'seeling night' to hide it.

context.history: To 'seel' was a falconer's term for stitching shut a young hawk's eyes to tame it; Macbeth asks night to blind the day.

significance: The couple's roles have reversed since Act I: she now counsels calm, he plans alone. The imagery of snakes, scorpions and night shows a mind poisoned by its own crime.

anchorPassages.note: Desire without content; the dead sleep while the living torture themselves.
anchorPassages.text:
Nought’s had, all’s spent,
Where our desire is got without content:
’Tis safer to be that which we destroy
Than by destruction dwell in doubtful joy.
Enter Macbeth.
How now, my lord! why do you keep alone,
Of sorriest fancies your companions making,
Using those thoughts which should indeed have died
With them they think on? Things without all remedy
Should be without regard: what’s done is done.
We have scotch’d the snake, not kill’d it:
She’ll close and be herself, whilst our poor malice
Remains in danger of her former tooth.
But let the frame of things disjoint, both the worlds suffer,
Ere we will eat our meal in fear and sleep
In the affliction of these terrible dreams
That shake us nightly: better be with the dead,
Whom we, to gain our peace, have sent to peace,
Than on the torture of the mind to lie
In restless ecstasy. Duncan is in his grave;
After life’s fitful fever he sleeps well;
Treason has done his worst: nor steel, nor poison,
Malice domestic, foreign levy, nothing,
Can touch him further.

Hath rung night’s yawning peal, there shall be done
A deed of dreadful note.
What’s to be done?
Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck,
Till thou applaud the deed. Come, seeling night,
Scarf up the tender eye of pitiful day;
And with thy bloody and invisible hand
Cancel and tear to pieces that great bond
Which keeps me pale! Light thickens; and the crow
Makes wing to the rooky wood:
Good things of day begin to droop and drowse;
Whiles night’s black agents to their preys do rouse.
Thou marvell’st at my words: but hold thee still:
Things bad begun make strong themselves by ill.
So, prithee, go with me.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Nought’s had, all’s spent, / Where our desire is got without content” slowly and put it in my own words: Lady Macbeth says nothing is gained and everything is spent when desire is achieved without contentment. Next, craft. I notice the balanced, rhyming phrasing that sounds like a sad proverb. The strongest word is “content”: it means peace of mind, which their crime has destroyed. Then, effect. What does Lady Macbeth realize about their success? My answer: She realizes their ambition has brought only unhappiness; the line shows her early regret, though she hides it from Macbeth.

Useful evidence: “Nought’s had, all’s spent, / Where our desire is got without content” (Act III, Scene II, lines 1103–1104): Lady Macbeth's despair. Theme link: both are unhappy: "Nought's had, all's spent." Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.
